title: Dynamic SQL
description: Build SQL statements at runtime using sp_executesql, parameterize queries safely, and prevent SQL injection attacks.

data.text: Sometimes you cannot know the table name, column name, or filter value at the time you write the query. You might need to query a table whose name is passed as a parameter, or build a WHERE clause dynamically based on user input. That is where *dynamic SQL* — constructing and executing SQL statements at runtime as strings — comes in.

The sp_executesql system stored procedure executes a T-SQL statement. The statement must be a Unicode string prefixed with N. Unlike the older EXEC, sp_executesql supports parameterized queries, which is critical for both performance and security.

data.title: Basic sp_executesql
Always use N prefix
data.text: SQL Server expects Unicode strings for dynamic SQL. Always prefix with N: N'SELECT ...'. Without it, non-ASCII characters and certain collation behaviors can cause silent issues.

The real power of sp_executesql is parameter binding. You pass the parameter definition and values separately from the SQL string, which allows SQL Server to reuse the cached plan across different parameter values.

data.title: Parameterized query with sp_executesql

data.text: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated directly into a SQL string. An attacker can append '; DROP TABLE users; -- to a user-supplied table name and execute it alongside your query.

data.title: Vulnerable vs. safe dynamic SQL
Safe: use QUOTENAME for object names
QUOTENAME prevents injection
data.text: QUOTENAME wraps the input in square brackets and escapes any embedded closing brackets: [production.brands;DROP TABLE sales.tests] — the injected SQL becomes part of the object name, and the statement fails instead of executing both parts.
A common pattern: build a WHERE clause dynamically based on which filters the caller specified, then execute the assembled query with sp_executesql.

data.title: Dynamic WHERE from optional parameters
Dynamic SQL trade-offs
data.text: Dynamic SQL is powerful but harder to read, harder to debug, and a common surface for SQL injection. Only use it when static SQL cannot express the logic. Prefer parameterized queries, always use QUOTENAME for object names, and thoroughly review the final @sql string before execution.

data.title: Dynamic SQL essentials
points: Use sp_executesql (not EXEC) for parameterized dynamic SQL — it enables plan reuse
Always prefix strings with N for Unicode, and always pass N for the parameter-definition string
Use QUOTENAME for object names to prevent SQL injection
Build WHERE clauses dynamically by appending conditions and parameters separately
Dynamic SQL is harder to debug — prefer static SQL when possible
